Current reinforcement learning (RL) methods predominantly assume tasks remain constant or are completely independent, often neglecting the capacity of agents to accumulate cross-task experiences. This limitation hinders their effectiveness in real-world scenarios where costs associated with data collection and computational training make fresh experiences hard to secure. To address this, we introduce Lifelong Evaluation for Real-world Tasks using Lifelong Learning and Simulation (L2Explorer), a novel RL benchmark designed to foster agents capable of discovering, retaining, and transferring knowledge across a sequence of changing tasks. Our proposal incorporates generated task sequences via Markov chains, features distinct reward delays for each individual task, and employs a dynamic task-closing mechanism to encourage continuous learning rather than complete forgetting after a task ends. Tests within this environment across state-of-the-art RL algorithms indicate that experience-based agents can indeed mitigate sample inefficiency and enhance learning efficiency by leveraging prior knowledge from prior tasks. Additionally, we evaluate strategies for constructing generated task sequences and Introspective State Representation (ISR) by comparing how different agents respond to collapsed versus distinct task states, revealing that weaker agents tend to overfit to specific tasks, whereas stronger agents develop true lifelong capabilities to continuously adapt. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the promise of L2Explorer as a generative framework for evaluating progress in continuous learning under RL.

The first phase aims to develop a versatile software architecture capable of handling all nine configurations, with an additional ten enhancement modules to be added later, bringing the total number of combinations to twenty. This work examines time-localized, analytic flow connections between time-periodic wave solutions and nearby 2D zonal (mean) flows. Adapted from finite-depth water wave theory, these structures include a wave–flow component similar to surface waves paired with a mean flow element analogous to average surface transport. We adapt this model into the context of 2D inviscid Euler equations by interpreting the mean flow as a near-zonal (zonal-averaged) flow. Utilizing a dual Gallay-Lüer-Jeydelsch (Gallay-Lühr-Veeren) approach, we identify a non-empty invariant manifold of analytic solutions near a zonal state consisting entirely of time-periodic waves. We further detail the structure of this manifold through an expansion in terms of analytic normal forms.

We introduce the field theory for exciton-polariton condensates, demonstrating that nonlinearity arises exclusively from a four-wave mixing process involving two optical modes and two nonlinear modes characterized by a distinct energy gap. This process accounts for optical mode saturation through an interaction with nonlinearity. Using the proposed theory, we derived analytical expressions for steady-state solutions representing either a single mode or coupled modes. We found that while saturation drives mode competition by equalizing nonlinearity, it can also balance saturation by distributing population evenly across modes when polariton energies are symmetrized. Additionally, we developed all-optical methods to manipulate linear polarization in systems containing either two optical modes. In a single-mode scenario, linear polarization stability results from balancing nonlinearity; conversely, in a two-component system, linear polarization arises from equibrating nonlinearity and population due to energy gap constraints. These predictions suggest practical realizations in bose-einstein-like energy-well structures composed of excitons and dark matter particles.

In early 2020, the South African Health Products Regulatory Agency (SAHPRA) maintained a database tracking COVID-19 cases, yet the agency faced criticism for not making the data accessible to the public. To address this limitation, a team of computer scientists utilized the agency's data format to develop an open-source data visualization tool to track the pandemic. This study examines the development of this SAIDD tool, highlighting how the development team's commitment to open-source principles enabled the project team to use critical data visualization libraries to build the tool. This study also examines how the development team's dedication to making their code available to the public enabled community members to use critical contributions to build the tool. This study concludes by discussing the value of using a community-driven approach to build the tool, emphasizing that such methods enable public health experts to provide critical feedback to build the tool, ensuring it meets the needs of stakeholders.

This paper introduces a new dataset comprising fundus images and Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) scans annotated for glaucoma as well as diabetic retinopathy by medical experts. While glaucoma involves damage to the optic nerve, which is often visualized via OCT, retinopathy manifests as retinal lesions visible in fundus photos. Consequently, we have updated and evaluated classification models using this multi-modal data to distinguish between these two conditions, and our performance results have surpassed existing state-of-the-art methods. The complete dataset can be accessed at https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/abdulkaderglaucomedrd.

The ongoing global pandemic, driven by the emerging SARS-CoV-2 virus, has resulted in an unprecedented surge in ICU admissions, placing an unsustainable strain on healthcare systems worldwide. As healthcare providers face a shortage of diagnostic resources like personal protective equipment, ventilators, and medical staff, the need for scalable solutions becomes critical. While extensive clinical data—including patient demographics, vital signs, and treatment records—are available, diagnostic capabilities are often limited to the visual inspection of CT or X-ray images by specialists. This study introduces a novel, data-driven methodology to correlate these radiographic findings with clinical records using a machine learning framework. By leveraging advanced techniques, we uncover specific features within the images that correlate strongly with actual patient data. The proposed model achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) score of 0.8583, accurately predicting features such as the need for ventilator support and blood oxygen levels based on scan imagery. These findings not only validate the effectiveness of our approach but also identify precise radiographic markers linked to severe COVID-19 outcomes, potentially informing the design of cost-effective, deployable systems for resource-constrained environments.

User intent discovery remains a pivotal challenge in dialogue systems, where accurately deciphering user objectives from historical interaction transcripts is essential for structuring conversational turns. Nevertheless, existing models are limited by treating intent recognition as zero-shot task, often lacking the capability to distinguish between unseen or emerging purposes that emerge post-deployment. This research introduces PAID (Pre-training Alignment Intention Discovery), a novel approach designed for emerging intent detection through two phases: pre-training and inference (alignment). During pre-training, we employ pre-trained language models to align domain-specific knowledge by jointly optimizing word embeddings with semantic dialogue representations. In the inference stage, emerging intents are identified by calculating the alignment score between isolated utterance representations and various intent labels. Leveraging the word embeddings derived from our proposed pre-training algorithm significantly enhances performance on both emerging intent detection and the broader task of intent discovery. Empirical evaluations on two public datasets, along with real-world instances from actual chat applications, demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of our method's training alignment strategy.

Let G be a fixed simplicial group. For any pair of simplicial sets, we define the Borel construction as the associated diagonal simplicial set from the product of G with the function space into that object. Consequently, the simplicial collection C_G is formed by taking global sections from the resulting diagonal object applied in a varying dimension to that of the domain. It is shown that for any two such sets, this simplified collection C_G maintains the same Simeplicial homotopy type as the collection derived from the diagonal of the product of G with the function space into that object. Specifically, we demonstrate that this collection C_G inherently carries the structure of a simplicial group and establishes an equivalence to the case where G is an abelian simplicial group, effectively showing it is a simplicial abelian group. Furthermore, we prove that this construction C_G naturally forms a simplicial group homofunctor on the category of simplicial sets, which maps to the simplified diagonal of the product. Finally, we illustrate an application of this universal simplicial group in the field of simplicial homotopy theory.

The Hunter–Tulczyjew "H2" study introduced a dimensionless variant of the Kreiss–Chisnell formalism specifically for perfect gases; this formula has since become a standard tool for investigating the fundamental characteristics of shock-induced shocks and numerous other phenomena related to shock waves. Building on their earlier work, we expand upon and offer an expanded overview of the Kreiss–Chisnell approach to examine how the H2 equation applies within the context of shocks and other phenomena. We begin by outlining the Kreiss–Chisnell method, after which we present a detailed analysis of the H2 equation itself. Next, we explore its usage in modeling the four principal features of shocks and the associated phenomena, before finishing with a discussion of the formula's inherent limitations.

Visual relationship detection (VRD) focuses on identifying interactions between objects in an image. While recent advancements have largely improved recall, addressing the persistent issue of low precision remains pivotal for further VRG system evolution. This paper introduces two novel strategies to diminish false positives in VRG detection, achieving a cumulative gain of 0.024 in Predicted Average Precision Improvement (Pred AP). The first method leverages global image context to construct spatial-aware relationship features, enhancing feature discrimination through mechanisms like global attention to generate context-aware embeddings, thereby reducing ambiguity. In parallel, a data augmentation technique targeting positive samples is developed to strengthen model robustness against false positives by expanding the diversity of valid relationship instances. Together, these approaches yield a statistically significant improvement in Visual Relationship Detection performance.

This research demonstrates that based on the refined correlation concepts, the entanglement structure of the initial state is no longer a strict prerequisite; rather, what matters is the price paid for weak-measurement operations. Consequently, these affordable operations enable the generation of quantum correlations between qubits, provided the weak-measurement cost remains below the entanglement cost of the underlying state. This analysis reveals that weak-measurement-abled quantum correlations can emerge from, and exist independently of, entanglement in the initial state since the weak-measurement price falls between zero and the entanglement cost of the target state. This provides a formal distinction, showing that affordable weak-measurement operations allow quantum correlated outcomes without requiring entanglement. Typically, social attributes are inferred in video by analyzing individual trajectories. However, defining relationships based solely on trajectories is often ambiguous. This paper presents an intermediate step: a machine learning network directly mapping people and their paths to constructing a Social Relationship Graph (SRG). Communication Passing Networks (CPNs) are increasingly popular for modeling complex vision recognition tasks, yet existing approaches rely on fixed full or semi-sparse strategies for communication scheduling, lacking the flexibility to adapt to varying scenarios. In response, this paper proposes Dynamic Graph Communication Passing Network (DGCPN), a novel CPN architecture designed to learn scenario-adaptive strategies for scheduling communication. DGCPN reimagines communication as a series of dynamic information flows between nodes governed by independent, flexible schedules. By learning the importance of individual dimensions within these communication processes, our model can effectively address diverse visual challenges such as visual question answering and visual relationship detection without manual design biases. Extensive experimental validation on prominent benchmarks confirms DGCPG's superior performance and strong generalization capabilities. Furthermore, visualization results demonstrate its capacity to capture intricate semantic relationships while avoiding overfitting.

Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) is a critical operation in numerous signal processing applications, typically implemented using a combination of hardware multipliers, shifters, and adders/subtractors. This work presents two novel methods for calculating MCMs with integers that significantly reduce hardware costs by minimizing the count of required multipliers, along with optimizing the counts of adders and subtractors. Initially, we introduce a new algorithm designed to determine the minimum number of multipliers needed for a given set of constants. By building on this approach, we develop a comprehensive flow for integer MCM realignment. These tools were evaluated against existing multi-purpose methods and previous technical benchmarks, demonstrating that they deliver results comparable to current state-of-the-art methodologies.

Deep learning's recent dominance has stemmed from its ability to deliver superior outcomes in numerous tasks, largely due to surges in computing capabilities and data availability that enabled the training of increasingly complex models. Initially introduced by LeCun et al. in 1990 as Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), deep learning models proved highly effective for sequence processing but faced inherent limitations regarding long-term dependencies, a defect later remedied by Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units proposed by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber in 1997. More recently, quantum computing has emerged as a promising avenue for advancing sequence analysis capabilities following the demonstration of quantum advantages over classical methods in specific scenarios. However, current applications remain confined to isolated use cases. This review examines two primary obstacles preventing the widespread deployment of quantum deep learning models: the absence of theoretically proven structural designs and the practical limitations of near-term quantum hardware. Finally, the paper outlines prospective research trajectories aimed at overcoming these barriers and facilitating future advancements in the field.

We investigate the characteristics of linearized waves within both causal and acausal frameworks of viscary relativistic fluid dynamics, focusing on the impacts of various viscary closures. Traditional approaches, which construct viscary fluid dynamics initially ignoring causality and subsequently imposing causal constraints via adjustments to relaxation times or coefficients, are assessed. These methods yield a partial relaxation of multiple diffusion modes that were previously non-causal. We argue, however, that this tactical order creates an artificial resolution causing the miss of physically motivated diffusion modes capable of becoming causal independently. Instead, a unified development approach—simultaneously addressing conservation laws and constitutive relations while remaining agnostic to specific causal realization strategies—is proposed. This methodology enables a comprehensive, side-by-side comparison of diffusion modes arising from multiple sources to confirm their collective causality. Such an analysis offers a detailed roadmap for designing causal fluid dynamics models, optimizing model parameters through a detailed examination of the density dependence of the rate of change of entropy, particularly in high-energy collisions where fluid dynamics is extensively utilized.

This study calculates the spectral characteristics and angular distribution of gamma-ray backgrounds produced by primordial black holes (PBHs) evaporating into high-energy particles, with a focus on scenarios where energy release is dominated by muons and subsequent decay gamma-rays. The resulting angular spectrum peaks sharply at very high energies around 10 TeV, causing detectability only for massive clusters like those weighing approximately $100^4~M_{\odot}$. Additionally, the paper addresses the generation of ultra-high-energy (UHE) cosmic rays via PBH evaporation. It specifically examines the contribution from the direct emission of protons/neutrons and gamma-ray final states that decay into hadronic particles, finding that UHE cosmic ray flux from these mechanisms far exceeds observed limits set by experiments such as the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array. This paper proposes the Virtual Safeguard Platform, a sophisticated software architecture designed to ensure secure computation in an untrusted environment. By leveraging Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE), this platform isolates users from remote malicious attacks, allowing private data uploads to execute securely on remote servers without exposure. The core innovation lies in its dual-functionality: it operationally emulates target applications while simultaneously executing their corresponding security verification tests concurrently. If a malicious app behavior is detected, the corresponding safe emulation remains hidden until confirmation by FTEE, ensuring threat containment. Furthermore, it can enforce access controls, protecting users from both external threats and internal malicious actors. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through the successful concurrent execution and verification of two specific applications, Mozilla Firefox and VLC Player, implemented entirely over the Threshold Fully Homomorphic Encryption scheme.

Pretrained language models, such as BERT and GPT, have achieved significant success across numerous natural language processing tasks. However, their evaluation methods remain limited, primarily focusing on task-level assessment using standard metrics like accuracy or F1 scores. Additionally, most existing work adopts a supervised approach, often requiring scarce high-quality training annotations. To address these issues, this paper introduces Unsupervised and Few-shot Analysis, a new framework designed to assess what a pretrained language model can do without additional supervision or training data, thereby identifying inherent capabilities already embedded within the model. We demonstrate this approach using the Hugging Face transformer model, which is based on the GPT-2 architecture. We propose three distinct analysis tasks: relation extraction, slot filling, and natural language inference. For each, we outline experimental setups, demonstrate evaluation procedures, and present illustrative cases. Ultimately, these findings reveal that substantial potential exists across all three tasks directly in GPT-2's parameters, which can be liberated through simple prompt engineering.

Cityscape images are enriched with rich details such as buildings, roads, and vegetation, yet utilizing them fully has been restricted by a lack of precise labeling techniques. However, cityscape cameras now have the ability to capture spectral information across multiple wavelengths. This capability allows for the automatic classification of objects through spectral signatures, effectively turning raw spectral data into meaningful semantic labels. This study proposes a deep learning approach for semantic segmentation driven by spectral signatures with only partial supervision. This method employs two distinct but separate classification modules: the first interprets RGB visuals, and the other analyzes the spectral data. By leveraging self-supervised learning, each module extracts features independently using their respective input types. These features are then merged to produce the final segmented output. Experiments conducted on cityscape datasets indicate that, despite utilizing minimal ground truth annotations, this model performs on par with, or better than, fully supervised state-of-the-art methods.

We establish a set of graph homology theories equipped with differential shapes—a valence-distinguished invariant composed of twisted differential forms and vector fields—that generate two forms of integration. Applying this framework allows for a differential form- and period-based interpretation of massless Feynman integrals. Specifically, along rapidly converging toy models, this approach yields explicit expressions for both the logarithmic transcendental valence and non-rational components of these integrals. Furthermore, extending this methodology suggests a new perspective on mass-dependent contributions, offering a conceptual model for the photon self-energy diagram at order $\mathcal{O}(1)$.

Previous research suggests that object traits like shape, texture, and material are treated as independent visual cues during early processing in both the brain and existing AI architectures. However, during later stages of learning in deep systems, these traits often diverge from orthogonality, meaning their informational content starts to overlap significantly. This study demonstrates that in recurrent object-detection models categorized by object traits, category-independent (orthogonal) traits actually enhance performance. Specifically, we found that when trained on the COCO dataset to prioritize category-orthogonal object features, these models not only maintained or improved their object detection accuracy but also exhibited faster convergence and sustained higher precision. Additionally, the model parameters developed through this method displayed greater robustness to corrupt.

This paper investigates a one-dimensional non-Hermitian lattice model featuring dissipation-driven dissipation-induced many-body correlations, specifically examining their impact on point-gap topology. We demonstrate that, unlike independent-site effects, this dissipation-induced topology arises exclusively many-body interactions. Furthermore, we show that correlations enable the system to bypass point-gap barriers, thereby nullifying the associated topological number. As the control parameter varies, the system exhibits a phase transition; we analyze these transitions by evaluating both the spectral and dissipative structures, as well as the time-local phase. Crucially, we find that tracking the time-local phase provides an experimentally viable method for detecting these dissipation-induced topological changes.

This research extends the concept of Polyphase Golay Complementary Arrays (PGCA) to configurations defined by design parameters $m$ and $k$ where both are coprime to each other. While prior research primarily focused on the case where $k$ divides a power of $m$, our approach leverages roots of unity filters (RUF) to generate PGCA structures for general coprime pairs, providing proofs for both sufficient and necessary conditions. We further introduce two novel family construction methods (FCCMs)—specifically Sum Rule Family and Difference Rule Family—which establish PGCA existence for all two variables that share a common factor. These methods are demonstrated through multiple examples, including new PGCA instances derived from $a \times a$ Golay Complementary Arrays (GCA) for dimensions 15, 27, and 37. Additionally, we present verified upper bounds on the total count of possible Golay Complementary Arrays.

This study examines On-Shell (OS) and Off-Shell (OS) production of the Higgs boson within the final state of four leptons, leveraging data from CMS at the LHC, which corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 137 fb$^{-1}$ collected at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. The analysis incorporates standard Model predictions alongside modifications such as anomalous Higgs boson-$W/Z$-couplings and constraints on the Higgs boson's total decay width. By comparing data to SM simulations, limits are established for the non-standard parameters. Furthermore, constraints on the Higgs boson's total width, $\Gamma_{h\to\gamma\gamma}$, are derived using the ratio of Off-Shell to OS production cross-sections in the four-lepton channel, yielding upper bounds of approximately 75 GeV (95% CL) under a pure SM hypothesis and between 40 and 80 GeV under the anomalous coupling framework.

Detecting changes between two co-registered hyperspectral images is a critical task with broad utility across multiple disciplines. While various methodologies have been explored, most rely on fusing spectral data from both images to identify discrepancies. In this study, we present an unsupervised framework that integrates spectral information with spatial and temporal characteristics through FeFuDNCNet, a convolutional neural architecture designed specifically for change identification. The process begins by extracting spectral features and the key points of interest (KPOIs)—which encompass spatial and temporal data—from both input datasets. These extracted features are then combined to construct a fused representation that captures interdependencies among different data modalities; this representation drives the detection logic. Experiments conducted on the RSCIES dataset demonstrated that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, achieving an overall accuracy of 90.2% and an OA of 88.2%.

In this study, we explore silicon's atomic-scale setup for interference between valley states and spin. By positioning a single adatom within an engineered quantum dot defined by gallium gates, we monitor the quantized conductance as we vary both the Gausssian screening and the magnetic field. Our results reveal that Gausssian tuning drives an atomic-scale resonant switch capable of exchanging spin states via a mechanism of valley interference. Furthermore, we map the phase acquired during this spin exchange as a function of position within the dot and the applied magnetic field. These findings represent crucial observations for valley-mediated operations essential to future quantum computing architectures based on silicon.

Optimization methods remain a vital research focus across numerous disciplines. Historically, this field has been hindered by a scarcity of specialized software tools, forcing practitioners to rely on multipurpose general-purpose packages that often fall short in handling specific, nuanced requirements. Built upon a robust architectural design, the platform facilitates both the consumption of optimization algorithms and the custom creation of new variants or advanced features. This capability enables researchers to validate hypotheses about optimal strategies by allowing for the rapid development of prototypes, a process that would otherwise demand extensive manual coding efforts.

We introduce a two-photon absorption edge transient-voltage technique that enables the direct visualization and measurement of charge transport within three dimensions. Using this method, we mapped the drift velocities of both holes and electrons across a single diamond crystal across magnetic fields ranging from 0 to 4 Tesla across temperatures of 78 K and 300 K. These experimental results were compared with direct measurements obtained from pulsed voltage experiments, demonstrating excellent alignment with the data reported in established literature.

This study introduces a computational approach to identifying and classifying misogyny in Arabic social media content. Given the scarcity of pre-trained models capable of arabic tokenization, we first developed and integrated several custom models for tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, and argument mining into a deep multi-tack architecture designed for text classification. This integration was specifically applied to a misogyny detection task using an annotated dataset covering Arabic tweets. The resulting model outperformed both standalone components and other relevant solutions. Furthermore, we evaluated the effectiveness of various embeddings, including those pre-trained on Arabic corpora. To address data sparsity, which often limits the generalizability of these embeddings, we implemented a data augmentation technique using the AugmentT5 model. Although this increased training set volume, our results indicated that such augmentation ultimately negatively impacted classification performance.

This paper presents fresh existence and uniqueness findings for nonlinear, postponed fractional backward stochastic differential equations. Our proof relies primarily on the technique of approximation combined with the A priori estimation method. These results significantly generalize and extend several earlier studies found in the literature.

The increasing complexity of cyber-physical systems (CSPs) necessitates the use of sophisticated control strategies. However, traditional model-based methods often fail due to the high dimensionality of these systems' state and control spaces. This paper proposes a novel solution by integrating policy search with probabilities. Drawing inspiration from recent policy search applications in deep reinforcement learning, which rely on sample-based estimation policies, this approach replaces the sample-based reliance with a learned system model to enable more efficient learning. Since perfect system models are rarely available, the method incorporates an imperfect policy to account for modeling uncertainties, a decision supported by theoretical analysis. To ensure robustness against such uncertainties, the contribution of the decision theory to the problem is the development of the Coupled Posterior Expectation Cost (CEC), the primary tool for the CSP's risk assessment. Empirical validation of the approach is provided by applying it to two standard, high-complexity CSPs: the swing equation and the swing pendulum problem.

Secure control ensures that dynamic systems adhere to safety constraints alongside control objectives. However, existing literature often neglects the real-time variability of these constraints in practical implementations. This paper introduces a configuration-aware secure control framework designed specifically for mobile robotic arms operating within unstructured environments. The core challenge lies in formulating a real-time control strategy for the arm's trajectory planner while accounting for the uncertainty in obstacle locations. Our proposed solution employs Model Predictive Control (MPC) integrated with control barrier functions (CBFs). Traditional MPC formulations often overlook constraint dynamics or resolve conflicts only post-optimization. In contrast, our approach incorporates relative control barrier functions directly into the MPC cost function, enabling real-time compliance with barrier certificates. Furthermore, by incorporating control Lyapunov functions, the method optimally balances safety goals with performance. Simulation results validate the arm's capability to navigate navigational paths safely within a non-structured workspace populated with random obstacles.

Weather conditions profoundly affect human activities, ranging from daily routines to global operations like transportation, commerce, and agriculture, alongside impacts on health and safety; therefore, effective management of these effects relies on accurate, prompt weather categorization. Although numerous automated systems exist to classify weather using visible data, this study seeks to determine the most suitable dataset and evaluate the best Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures for this task. To address data scarcity, we introduce the novel "Capture Clouds and Sunlight" (CCaS) dataset, which consists of 1,000 images of sun and cloud scenes captured via a smartphone camera, organized into ten distinct categories aligned with standard meteorological definitions. A comprehensive evaluation comparing various CNNs on the new CCaS dataset is also provided, alongside a detailed analysis of their performance on this unique resource.

This study examines how Science, Institutions, and Economics intersect regarding climate change to analyze social norms surrounding science and its societal impact. It asks how scientific practices, societal structures, and economic theories connect to shaping norms about climate change, and what effect those norms have on society. Research shows that while scientific and institutional factors primarily drive the formation of these norms, their origins in science and within institutions matter less than the norms' content and function in shaping behavior. Specifically, while public support for climate change science is broad, understanding remains shallow; institutional backing for research is strong, yet political pressure weakens support for teaching climate change. Consequently, climate change standards directly influence social action, polarize based on individual values, and serve as a barometer for that values' distribution. In economics, though there is consensus on climate change risks and optimal policies, this consensus rarely forms the basis of policy formation, which instead relies on short-term political considerations. Ultimately, while risk perception varies, policy decisions appear guided more by immediate gains than by long-term environmental strategy, with self-interested policy promotion reinforcing their respective interests to advance specific agendas.

This paper introduces a multi-modal neural network designed to predict outcomes in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). As the most prevalent lung malignancy affecting roughly 50% of all cases, lung cancer remains difficult to treat due to a lack of effective systemic therapies, resulting in a 5-year survival rate of only around 24%. Our proposed solution integrates four distinct clinical data modalities: electronic health records (EHR), radiological imaging (radiology), laboratory results (lab), and genetic information (genomics). EHR provides structured and unstructured patient data, including diagnoses and history; the imaging component utilizes multi-view medical scans, while genetic data draws from multiple types of biological markers. To address challenges with class imbalance in these diverse datasets, we implemented a data augmentation strategy based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Furthermore, a deep learning-based feature extraction method was developed to harmonize the genomics and radiology data. This model, enhanced with an attention mechanism to prioritize the most critical features for each modality, combines all processed data for the final prognostic prediction. Experimental outcomes, validated against a benchmark comparison method, demonstrate the proposed neuro-prognostic net's superior performance. Specifically, the new net's C-index of 0.7830 significantly surpasses the 0.7100 achieved by a standard Cox Proportional Hazards model, indicating robust predictive validity.

Current open-ended dialogue models struggle to maintain coherent or relevant conversations due to their lack of specific user role constraints. Previous efforts to assign user roles have resulted in poor role adherence, excessive repetitiveness, or insufficient historical context awareness. This study introduces an approach using advanced large-scale language models to define a user's role through backstories, with the goal of creating a more immersive chat experience. The proposed framework is evaluated across three key areas: the extent to which the resulting dialogue reflects the assigned role, the model's ability to utilize relevant conversation history, and the overall quality of the dialogue. The method's efficacy has been validated through automated assessments as well as human expert evaluations from across three specific dimensions. Empirical results demonstrate a superior performance over existing baseline methods in maintaining role consistency, conversational quality, and historical context awareness.

Gravitational wave memory represents a permanent change in proper distance between free-falling test masses induced by gravitational waves. Although this effect cannot be detected by current-frequency detectors like LIGO or Virgo because those instruments rely on oscillatory signals, the superposition of many individual memory events could create a stochastic background within the detectable band. This study calculates that rate to be $10^{-21} \text{ Hz}^{-1}$, which falls significantly short of LIGO-Virgo's sensitivity floor of $10^{-20}\text{-}10^{-19} \text{ Hz}^{-1}$. Consequently, even with present instrumentation, this stochastic memory background is unlikely to be observable.

This work presents a SUSY-breaking mechanism driven by a first-order phase transition occurring within a two-Higgs-doublet SUSY quiver model. Furthermore, we posit that the coexistence of PeV-scale black holes and supersymmetry can be explained, suggesting these objects may eventually be detectable via future gravitational wave observations and events taking place at the high-energy end of the gravitational spectrum.

User preference prediction is crucial for recommendation systems, as the rapid evolution of user behavior poses significant challenges. To address this, research has increasingly focused on session-based approaches that analyze short user interaction sequences. However, as sessions are extremely brief and contain few user actions, these methods struggle to build a robust sequence representation, often resulting in suboptimal performance. To resolve this issue, we introduce TSER (Two-Stage Recommender), a solution designed for session-oriented tasks. TSER utilizes a two-stage framework: the first stage generates recommendations, while the second stage filters them to enhance interaction. Specifically, we develop a Candidate Rank Embedging (CRE) technique that captures the ordering significance of items within sessions by generating item rank embeddings. Furthermore, we propose a series-based graph neural network to utilize historical user interactions for producing accurate candidate rank predictions. To tackle the imbalance between positive and negative samples in the filtering stage, we incorporate a focal loss function. Extensive experiments on three public recommendation datasets demonstrate that TSER significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baseline methods, with improvements of up to 10.43% HMMS and 14.89% MRR.

Active particles, such as self-propelled micro- and nanorobots, consume internal energy to sustain their motion and maintain internal order against entropy. While individual activity levels have been extensively analyzed regarding their impact on transport and phase transitions, there is limited understanding concerning how spatial variations in local activity dictate the behavior of particle assemblies. To address this, our computational study places dimers—colloidal pairs connected by a spring—within colloidal fluids subjected to activity gradients. We demonstrate that these entities experience net transport against the direction of increased activity; notably, the net flow is consistently reversed within the dimers. By combining our simulations with a coarse-grained theoretical model, we explain this motion through the transformation of translational energy into rotational movement via spring deformation, an effect that is amplified and directed against the activity gradient when hydrodynamic interactions are accounted for. Our findings provide a vital foundation for organizing fission events and driving material flows in collective swarming behaviors for future microswimmer technologies.

Although deep learning models are deployed widely in practice, their opacity and lack of explainability often hinder their broad adoption. Existing methods for explaining neural networks mostly assume full model transparency, a premise rarely met in real-world scenarios where deployed systems act as black boxes. This study introduces a new framework called Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer (ZKT) that bypasses these black-box limitations. The ZKT approach transfers a pre-trained model's capabilities to the task without requiring direct access to that model's internals or its training data. The method operates by extracting a surrogate model from the black box's input-output data, which is then adapted in zero-shot fashion to the target task via another surrogate. Evaluation on image classification and instance segmentation demonstrates that ZKT successfully captures the underlying capacity of prevalent commercial detectors, achieving competitive performance on a custom image segmentation benchmark when measured against the method used to create the training data. The implications of these findings for the practical deployment of segmentation models are explored in depth.

This study introduces a machine learning framework to address depth-camera calibration and pose estimation relative to the robot's end-effector, eliminating the need for external markers. The proposed system splits the task into two distinct phases: first, it employs supervised learning to train a network that adjusts the 3D extrinsic parameters of the depth camera based on camera-mounted features derived from image data. Second, it utilizes a separate network to predict the robot's pose by processing features extracted from the depth map. Both learning stages are guided by optimization functions grounded in geometric constraints within the robot arm structure and visual features of attached cameras. Geometric features serve as the regression target in the calibration phase, while a scene's point cloud acts as the input for pose estimation, with its predicted transformation compared against the known true pose from the motion controller to determine the loss value for optimization. Experimental outcomes confirm that the learned geometric calibration closely matches traditional methods, and the end-effector pose predictions achieve accuracy comparable to that of the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm after an initial alignment step derived from the calibrated features.

The study evaluates the technique through simulations, comparing it's performance against established approaches, while also applying it to observational data from a randomized clinical trial context where it successfully isolates potential interferences.

The emergence of spin-liquid states in magnetic systems is often closely linked to geometric frustration. In contrast, we identify a distinct mechanism where non-frustrated Heisenberg antiferromagnets on the honeycomb lattice manifest spin-liquid behavior via combined effects of magnetic field and anisotropy. By employing large-scale Monte Carlo simulations, we map the parameter space corresponding to various spin-liquid regimes. We find that applying a field perpendicular to the easy-plane direction can either generate or suppress these states. Detailed first-principles calculations on Bernal graphite (beta-graphite) confirm the existence of these tunable Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) phases in real materials, thereby establishing experimentally accessible pathways to explore quantum spin-liquid physics in this specific structural configuration.

Recent SRAM-based random number generators have claimed true randomness by leveraging inherent circuit variations and noise, though these claims are often disputed due to a lack of rigorous evidence. This letter introduces a novel, hardware-efficient SRAM-based TRNG that leverages read currents to expose designers to vulnerabilities caused by transistor variations and the need for margining. By demonstrating how supply voltage fluctuations during the sampling phase of digital standard cells correlate with output samples, we propose a TRNG architecture that utilizes the specific undervolting of supply voltage to amplify these variations. This approach offers a significant hardware advantage over traditional thermal noise sources or weak random number generators by eliminating extra analog circuitry. Validation through two commercial 28nm CMOS test chips, which included a dedicated TRNG, confirmed compliance with all ANSI/NIST standards for randomness.

Achieving atom-by-atom control over oxides on metal substrates facilitates magnetic ordering that extends across extensive areas at high temperatures. This phenomenon arises from interactions between antiferromagnetically coupled oxygen and metal atoms within the film, a connection governed by non-trivial quantum mechanics that enables both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic alignments. Consequently, this relationship offers a compelling system for multidisciplinary research in quantum physics, chemistry, and condensed matter physics, driving significant applications in technology.

This study presents a theoretical investigation into the probability distribution of a single atom subjected to optical laser cooling and confined within a dissipative one-dimensional optical lattice. By extending a previously developed master equation to this new context, we obtain an analytical expression for the atom's probability distribution. Numerical simulations are employed to examine the statistical properties of the atomic position and momentum. Our results reveal significant non-Gaussian behavior in these properties under specific conditions. Additionally, we observe that the system can exist in two distinct phases: one featuring a broad, Gaussian-like Gaussian distribution where statistical properties are controlled by dispersion, and another, more narrow phase where the distribution follows, and statistical outcomes are governed by, interference effects.

This study examines cryptocurrency trading connections, beginning with an analysis of the node degree distribution to identify the node types that are most central. These correlations are further temporalized to reveal how such relationships evolve over time, ultimately detecting recurring patterns within these shifts. Subsequently, the work investigates quadruple relationships within the network to uncover potential high-order dependencies; specifically, quadruple relations are mapped based on the connectivity of their constituent pairs, demonstrating that quadruples associated with high node degree exhibit spatial clustering. The final section extends these findings to explore the distribution and temporal evolution of negative relationships among nodes. Through an integrated look at both binary and multi-node interactions, the manuscript concludes by discussing the real-world financial implications of these results.

This study employs quantum chemical calculations to examine how zero-point vibrational energy influences the structural stability and potential energy surfaces of compact water and sulfuric acid clusters. By utilizing the variational Monte Carlo method with explicitly correlated permutationally invariant polynomials, we assess various computational strategies for zero-point correction. Our findings indicate that incorporating quadratic potential approximations yields substantially more precise values compared to traditional density functional theory or harmonic perturbation theory approaches. These advanced methods also facilitate the investigation of anhartricity effects within these systems. Specifically, for the most stable configurations of water clusters comprising up to ten molecules and sulfuric acid dimers and trimers, we achieve calculated stability enhancements due to zero-point motion that align closely with high-level benchmark data.

A foundational element in functorial approaches to isometry group representation theory involves considering spaces of non-expanding operators from a Riemannian manifold $M$ to itself, denoted as $dist(M):= \{f : M \to M \mid d f \leq 1 \}$. Equally fundamental are the spaces equivariant under a specific group action $G$, defined as the subset $dist_G(M):= \{f \in dist(M) \mid f(g \cdot x) = g \cdot f(x) \}$ for all $g \in G, x \in M \}$, containing only the operators that preserve this symmetry. In this short communication, various compactifications of these spaces are examined, yielding compact forms such as $ \bar{dist}_G (M) \ }$. A primary finding of the authors is that these compact spaces function as natural targets for limit maps arising from sequences of isometries of $M $. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that for any group $G$, these spaces constitute the maximal domain capable of accommodating such limit maps for that particular group. Additional properties and applications of these compact spaces are also discussed.

In this theoretical investigation, we explore fluid dynamical behaviors in both classical and quantum contexts with finite temperature and density. We analyze scenarios where a medium experiences simultaneous viscous and thermal gradients, observing a cross-coupling effect where heat flow generates a fluid vortex. This phenomenon, known as the *thermal Hall reaction*, causes fluid elements to rotate around the axis of the heat flux with an angular velocity proportional to the heat flux magnitude and the Carberry number, a dimensionless constant reflecting the medium's properties.

A pivotal contribution of our work is the critical examination of theoretical analogies linking viscous diffusion of momentum to the diffusive diffusion of heat, specifically demonstrating these models do not hold simultaneously for realistic media. Furthermore, we quantify Einstein-type relations governing Brownian motion within the viscous, thermal environment, revealing that the traditional analogy fails to represent the dynamics of a particle whose diffusion is driven by thermal noise to within approximately 44 percent accuracy. These findings underscore the complexities inherent in extending classical fluid models to conditions including finite temperature and density, particularly regarding momentum and energy transport coupling.

A key open question regarding deep learning concerns the ease with which simple models generalize well and are found by optimizers, despite the theoretical expectations that deep neural networks should incur high representational costs for equivalent tasks. Drawing on connections between these representational theories and inductive biases, the authors investigate this phenomenon through the lens of geometric complexity, which measures the "flatness" of the loss landscape. They establish theoretical constraints: for both linear and nonlinear models, data correlations strongly dictate geometric complexity. Specifically, the signal's variance of the last layer weights correlates with how the optimum aligns with class labels, while an average cross-covariance with labels drives the optimization path. Learning rules based on gradient descent naturally descend toward minimal loss while preserving the linear model's last layer variance and mirroring the training path of more expressive models in terms of cross-covariance. Experimentally, the methodology was validated using linear classifiers and convolutional networks on MNIST, where measured geometric complexity aligns perfectly with the predicted theoretical bounds.

This study demonstrates that a link between a particle's intrinsic spin and its statistical behavior in the limit of $s\to0$ arises primarily from parities being multi-valued under the rotation group. Consequently, the parities of identical particles must commute with one another and interact solely through statistical phases. Under these conditions, the only consistent possibilities for these statistical phases are $\pm1$, distinguishing between bosons and fermions. Notably, this approach does not rely on the representation theory of the permutation group $S_N$, the postulate of complete symmetry, or the assumption of spatial wave function properties in the derivation. Instead, it offers an alternative representation of symmetric and anti-symmetric multi-particle states via Young's formalism, utilizing the Pauli algebra to enforce statistical phases without requiring explicit state exchange. Furthermore, this framework clarifies why half-integer spin particles exhibit the specific exclusion principles characteristic of fermions.

We introduce a modified RingCT variant called dRCT, where conditional logic based on policy allows networks to restrict transactors using invalid ring members for anonymity. The design addresses technical hurdles involving trusted setup, key management, and snafus like false negatives or inaccurate threshold signatures. The result is that the original RingCT protocol evolves into dRCT without sacrificing any of the latter's security guarantees. The challenge is to balance accuracy and speed in the design, where inaccurate signatures could result in false negatives and inaccurate threshold signatures could result in false positives. The technical solution is that dRCT inherits all the security guarantees provided by RingCT. The design also addresses challenges related to key management and the accurate verification of policy compliance and invalid transactions, ensuring no inaccurate results occur. dRCT is thus an extension of RingCT that provides faster transaction processing.

A key component is the Lanc-Lanc-Lon method, which identifies a vector $x$ such that $Ax-b$ has minimal norm. This work addresses multi-stage dynamic optimization by integrating data-driven relaxations at the boundaries of each time step. Our focus is on optimization models featuring polynomial equality and inequality constraints with basic variable domains defined as unions of multiple intervals. To enhance computational feasibility, we propose a new multi-stage optimization framework coupled with constraints that generate tailored McCormick envelope-based relaxations. These auxiliary constraints significantly reduce the complexity of the resulting non-convex multi-stage optimization problem by partitioning it into a series of smaller convex subproblems. Within a dynamic optimization setting, this design yields differential equation-based convex optimizations that can be formulated as sum-of-squares problems with Carleman expansions, ensuring a guaranteed level of approximation accuracy. Simulation results for the non-linear car-hitching benchmark demonstrate both the advantages and precise error bounds of this approach in dynamic optimization.

Recent research by Schraut, Cramer, and Gühne [Phys. Rev. A 101, 020201(R) (2020)] examined the probabilistic local operations and classical communication (LOCC) conversion between multipartite bound entangled states. Building on their findings, we introduce a new, more rigorous limitation on the probabilistic conversion of entangled states using the entropy of entanglement as its foundational metric. Our approach generalizes the well-known lower bound established by Bennett et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 82, 5299(1999)] for separable environments, extending it to arbitrary LOCC scenarios. This generalized lower bound is consistent with and explains the results derived by Schraut, Cramer, and Gühne. Furthermore, we clarify the relationship between this generalized constraint and the previously identified limitations proposed by Huber and Gühne [New J. Phys. 20, 033020 (2018)].

This research investigates the hydraulic behavior within a partially filled rectangular tank containing coffee undergoing horizontal oscillation, with objectives to explore teaching methodologies for undergraduate physics students and to advance comprehension of fluid dynamics in confined spaces. The study builds upon earlier research by combining experimental results with mathematical modeling to analyze tank sloshing, leveraging liquids with varying viscosities as surfactants. Although coffee's viscosity is negligible compared to water, adding surfactants allows for the creation of samples with measurable viscosities. Findings demonstrate that by altering viscosity, one can modify both the damped natural frequency and the q-factor, alongside observations of how adding volume and dimensions change tank characteristics, enabling calibration of natural frequencies. Decentralized learning has emerged as a cost-effective alternative to traditional machine training methods, offering significant gains in efficiency. However, standard approaches often fail to generalize effectively when training data is non-i.i.d., a common scenario in decentralized environments due to communication topologies that partition datasets. Additionally, the need to route information through intermediate nodes introduces privacy risks, as these nodes may lack secure operational protocols. To address these dual challenges, this paper introduces DR-DSGD, a robust training framework designed to mitigate distribution shifts while enabling secure data processing. DR-DSGD combines Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO)—which enhances model resilience against variations in data distributions with reweighting techniques—with two privacy-preservation methods. First, we demonstrate that applying ReWeighting individually at each intermediate node does not degrade learning performance despite the absence of i.i.d. assumptions. Second, to prevent the exposure of gradient information by such nodes, this work proposes an additive secret-sharing-based encryption scheme tailored for gradient vector addition in the context of Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets and network architectures validate the efficacy of this new algorithm.

We employ an AdS/C-inspired hydrodynamic framework to investigate fluid evolution following heavy-ion collisions. Within this context, we suggest utilizing entropy density as an ideal initial condition, a strategy capable of mitigally sensitivity to initial energy distributions. Additionally, we demonstrate that employing a critical exponents-based sound speed significantly influences the final entropy and particle number yields. We conclude by examining how varying initial entropies impact final particle multiplicities.

While high-velocity outflows are commonly observed in high-mass star formation, low-mass protostar star formation predominantly features low-velocity ejections, the cause of this difference is debated. This study investigates the underlying mechanisms by simulating low-velocity outflows with high-velocity jets using three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamohydrodynamic simulations (3D-MHD-HOH) focused on low-density regions. Specifically, the impact of high-velocity jets on mass ejection rates was examined. This study simulates a low protostellar jet with an initial velocity of approximately 100 kilometers per second. This high-velocity jet is observed to effectively mobilize surrounding circumstellar gas, creating extensive outflows with terminal velocities around 10 km/second. This demonstrates that high-velocity jet activity can play a significant role in initiating and driving outflows, a phenomenon that is consistent with previous studies.

This study addresses the problem of balancing performance and saturation limits in constrained nonlinear systems by deriving an equilibrium control strategy. This approach minimizes the ideal performance under hard constraints through relaxation techniques, subject to those constraints. To achieve this equilibrium, a novel performance evaluation metric based on a performance index and a constraint set is proposed. The performance of this equilibrium strategy is further analyzed by establishing performance certification conditions and constraint verification methods. Specifically, conditions certifying performance levels are formulated as parameterized linear matrix inequalities, while methods to confirm satisfaction of constraints are developed using feasibility checks.

This study presents generalised, closed-form expressions for the mean solar radiation pressure (SRP) perturbation caused by the $s$-th harmonic of the planet's orbital frequency, applicable to both equatorial and non-equatorial orbits. Utilizing these formulations, the paper identifies the condition equations for the resulting radiation force semi-secular resonances. These resonance types were previously examined only for an integrable, inertial model limited to planar motion; in contrast, the present work extends the analysis to include out-of-plane dynamics and the long-term effects of SRP perturbations on orbital elements regardless of inclination. To verify the predicted resonances, the authors conduct numerical simulations utilizing $J_2$ gravitational perturbations and integrate a $P_1$-model for SRP, thereby confirming the substantial influence of resonant terms on orbital inclination over time.

We demonstrate that within both inhomogeneous photonic crystals and systems featuring random matter-light coupling, electron density forms localized states bound to atoms, while optical modes either propagate freely or remain localized depending on their configuration. Despite this nontrivial structure, both numbers and spatial extents of these optical states are effectively determined simply as averages over random positions and configurations of the electrons. This outcome reflects a broader principle applicable to various disordered wave-scattering scenarios: the presence of invariance under transformations that permute potential sites leads to the measurement-scale independence of key spectral characteristics, despite the lack of global symmetry in the underlying Hamiltonian. Consequently, despite the random arrangement, key observables remain robust, relying solely on average density and range parameters rather than specific microscopic arrangements.

3D object reconstruction remains a pivotal challenge in Computer Vision. While prior research has largely concentrated on single-object instance reconstruction, this work targets Category-level Object Pose and Form (COPF) estimation, which simultaneously addresses the 3D shape and object pose for an entire category. To achieve this, we introduce the Keypoint-based COPF formulation, aiming to determine both shape and pose by aligning semantic keypoints. Consequently, we propose Keypoint-opt COPF, an objective function designed to optimize the pose-form estimation process. We further detail Key3D and Key2Net3D networks that facilitate keypoint-opt COPF execution through 2D keypoints and unstructured 3D keypoints, respectively. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets confirm the superiority of our approach over prior methods. Additionally, we release the datasets, source code, and model checkpoints to support future research.

Basket studies involve simultaneous recruitment of multiple patient subgroups受 to a singular experimental arm, enabling independent analyses across subgroups while simultaneously leveraging data to enhance estimation precision. By integrating information between these groups, these trials can ascertain sample size requirements more efficiently than traditional parallel designs. This study implements a Bayesian method to determine sample size in basket trials, simultaneously borrowing data to refine the sample volume necessary to achieve a pre-specified sample volume. It employs Bayes factors to measure the magnitude of this borrowing process and utilizes posterior distributions to evaluate trial success. We present numerical results using a posterior distribution and evaluate the method by examining how different levels of mean sharing impact the recommended sample volume and the posterior probability of achieving trial success.

This paper proposes a new model predictive control approach for high-precision motion systems designed to compensate for parameter uncertainties. Utilizing physical first-principles models, the design adopts an incremental Polytopic representation combined with specific constraints. Notably, innovative constraints are developed to mitigate planar errors arising from bending and axial deformation in these systems. By integrating these limitations into the optimization function, the method enhances following response accuracy. A distinctive feature of this architecture is its sequential loop tightening mechanism, which adaptively determines the control horizon based on the polytopic model's structure. Experimental validation using a motion table demonstrates an improvement in vertical positioning accuracy by approximately 30% compared to a standard approach that ignores physical effects.

Deep learning techniques for image registration have proven effective; however, most models rely on fully supervised approaches requiring paired whole images for training. This paradigm is often impractical in clinical settings due to registration drift over time and motion between scans. Regrettably, existing self-supervised methods predominantly focus on whole-image realignment, which is not always feasible due to patient movement or organ motion that prevents complete scan overlap. Although methods adapted for whole-image self-supervision exist, they often suffer from registration drift and are currently unavailable for the more general case of patch-based or partial-image alignment. In this paper, introduce PRNet, a self-supervised deep learning framework designed to align image fragments rather than complete scans. We empirically demonstrate through benchmarks that this approach is particularly well-suited for longitudinal pediatric cardiac MRI analysis.

In addition to laboratory settings, we explore other approaches for detecting the anomalous dimension of the Higgs operator, which enhances our understanding of the Standard Model's instability. Through a coarse-grained analysis, we assess the optimal strategies for identifying this additional term, which suggests the possibility of the Higgs potential becoming negative at high energy scales. Our analysis indicates that while no current or near-future collider can definitively confirm this operator's presence, the SM instability itself serves as a powerful motivator for constructing a machine more sensitive to it. Specifically, the proposed machine should surpass the capabilities of both the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) and any 100 TeV proton colliders, potentially reaching into the territory of high energy linear colliders to gather more precise data on the Higgs potential at high energy scales.

We introduce a method for reconstructing light-matter interaction potentials using time-resolved optical signals, specifically tailored for scenarios with significant noise or ambiguous data. Leveraging the concept of dynamical trajectories within an optical nonlinearity potential field, developed previously by the authors, this approach utilizes a finite trajectory basis to express both the unknown potential and the light field. While trajectory expansions for the potential have been utilized earlier, extending this technique to include the light field represents a novel contribution. This allows the formulation of data acquisition as an optimization problem along temporal trajectories, making the inverse sampling process an optimization task in the light field rather than the recovered potential. Consequently, the reconstruction task becomes a joint optimization of potentials and light fields, addressed simultaneously. This framework ensures that reconstructed fields satisfy the underlying optical propagation equations, even when based on imperfect experimental inputs. We demonstrate that a finite set of trajectories can be precomputed independently of specific data requirements. Furthermore, a conditional number analysis of the resulting Jacobian matrix reveals that carefully constructed trajectory bases exhibit well-conditioned properties, facilitating stable and efficient recovery. Numerical simulations, including cases with noisy measurements, validate the robustness and precision of this approach.

The paper provides the comprehensive and model-independent transverse momentum ($q_T$) distribution profiles for the $D$ meson families ($D$, $D_s$, $D_{ab}$), including those for the excited states $D^*$ and $D_s^*$. This formulation leverages bound state wave functions from non-relativistic potential models alongside the light-cone meson distribution amplitude. A key component is the novel determination of off-shell meson probabilities, defined as the squared values of the light-cone wave function at zero transverse momentum.

Current deep learning-driven instance segmentation techniques predominantly depend on dense pixel-level annotations for multiple input modalities, yet such labeled data are both expensive to acquire and difficult to secure. Moreover, these methods often exhibit poor generalization on both new classes and new modalities, necessitating retraining with modality-annotated training sets from target domains after deployment. Addressing these challenges, this paper introduces a groundbreaking solution that instancesegments unlabeled target modalities by leveraging labeled source domains without requiring any modality-specific annotation for the target data. Our approach, termed Cycle分割 GAN (Cycle Segmentation GAN), extends the CycleGAN framework by integrating a dedicated cycle consistency loss function tailored specifically for pixel-level alignment. This mechanism enables a powerful cross-domain instance segmentation capability: the model can extract instance boundaries in the target domain by cycling information from labeled source domains. Furthermore, a multi-domain extension is proposed to effectively utilize multiple source domains during training. Comprehensive experiments conducted across three datasets—two for monocular-color transfer (SUNBURST) and one for modalities injection (Pancreas) demonstrate that our method achieves performance on par with state-of-art techniques while avoiding the need for expensive instance annotation in the target domain.

To overcome limitations in feature extraction encountered by Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) when learning from raw inputs, this paper introduces Feature Mapping RNN (FM-RNN). This model leverages deep learning to learn features within an RNN framework, incorporating inductive regularities to reduce the dimensionality of hidden states while eliminating the need for backpropagation through time. By integrating the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel into the feature learning layer, FM-RNN becomes RBF-RNN, which benefits from the RBF's high nonlinearity and sparse property. Consequently, this integration enhances the model's feature learning and compression capabilities, leading to more efficient learning and superior performance in temporal action prediction. Experimental results on the THUMOS-14 and InfoR datasets confirm that the proposed RBF-RNN outperforms existing methods in terms of prediction accuracy.

On April 12, 1985, an intense stellar flare occurred in AD Leo, a young M4.5 star, producing the most intense recorded flaring event of any M-type star. This study utilizes comprehensive spectral data from near-ultraviolet (NUV) bands to model the spectral energy distribution (SED) of this phenomenon. Our simulation reveals a peak blackbody temperature of 13,000 K and a peak electron peak of $3.6 \times 10^{-13}$ K. The study also demonstrates the prominence of NUV radiation in flaring events of M-type stars, with our model showing a peak luminosity of $3.6 \times 10^{-13}$ Hz. This finding underscores the significance of NUV radiation in flaring events of M-type stars.

This study evaluates the use of Slotted ALOHA and CSMA for mediating access to massive device networks, a capability essential for detecting ranging and angular information in radar systems like those used for 3D localization. The primary goal is to mitigate collisions among transmitting devices, thereby lowering estimation errors and shortening the time needed to gather accurate estimates for all nodes. We analyze both approaches in terms of detection error, detection latency, and the overall duration of the detection process, demonstrating that networks employing these protocols result in a 40% to 70% reduction in detection time compared to unscheduled transmission methods.

This paper presents a theoretical analysis using spectral consideration to investigate the role of two-photon absorption in Hong-Ou-ML interference experiments. It demonstrates that when input photons experience Entangled Nonlinear (EntNl) media, the probability amplitude for finding both output photons on the same side is no longer zero, thereby deviating from standard classical behavior. For example, when half of the absorption occurs simultaneously for entangled photons in this context, the joint probability for co-localization at the beam splitter remains zero at the output. It demonstrates how this process leads to a reduction in the total intensity at the output port, as well as demonstrating that this process results in a change in sign probability for anti-bunching events. Finally, it discusses how this result provides insight into understanding photon-photon interactions via entangled nonlinear media, as well as their associated quantum correlation properties within such systems.

Temporal Knowledge Graph Inference (TKGI) aims to forecast missing Triplets consisting of entities and time intervals. A significant challenge within this domain is the lack of structured internal representations for time, which hampers the model's ability to capture inherent temporal dynamics. This study introduces a unified, low-rank, model-agnostic framework for representing time in TKGI. First, it constructs an explicit temporal operator by integrating pre-trained time embeddings into existing TKGI models. Second, it establishes links among time embeddings, time matrices, and knowledge triplets within the graph structure. Third, it imposes a low-rank constraint on these matrices to mitigate parameter overization and enhance generalization. Furthermore, the internal mechanisms governing time are made interpretable. Finally, experimental evaluations across three standard benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches.

This paper first outlines two noise generators for producing general presence sound, secondly presents two noise modifiers to specifically target metrical steps, and lastly, software is created to test if this approach enhances realism when heard.

This operational vehicle management platform, developed for commercial trucking, is designed to maintain primary driving functions following driver disengagement while ensuring safety amidst the loss of certain sensor capabilities. This paper presents the application of SPIN, a model-checking tool, to formally verify SPYRA's decision-making logic upon switch-over to this mode of operation. The study demonstrates that critical properties regarding safety and system integrity effectively cover a vast portion of the decision handler's state space.

Existing methods for dynamical systems clustering often fail to account for practical concerns, specifically real-time implementation, generalization across time, and the evaluation of temporal prediction accuracy. To address these gaps, this paper introduces a data-driven impact-based impact-based clustering (DBIC) framework. This system utilizes empirically derived impact events from available data to enable trajectory coupling, allowing trajectories to interact and exchange information whenever they approach within a defined distance threshold. Because the resulting dependency impact-based clustering relies solely on data-driven impacts, it offers a robust format for prediction that can be realized in real-time. This paper provides a rigorous mathematical framework that ensures the proximity of the resulting clusters while maintaining $ \varepsilon $-semidegeneracy (where $\varepsilon$ represents the maximum non-threshold separation). Additionally, dependency impact-based clustering exhibits uniform hyperbolicity, which guarantees the stability and $ \varepsilon $-smoothing of resulting clusters. We demonstrate the method's utility through detailed analyses applied to both simplified and high-fidelity models of the Earth-Moon system, as well as the 1988 World Table Tennis Championships final, where we also evaluate the method's performance.

This paper offers comprehensive studies of three approaches to calculus developed by Leibniz, including supporting historical context. We examine how these methods were modernized: in the cases of Warburton and d'Alembert by conforming to the rigorous standards of Weierstrassian analysis (emphasizing precision and formal definitions), versus in Leibniz Darboux adopting Cauchy's foundation (focusing on limits based on infinite proximity).

We apply disturbance theory to forecast signals from hydrogen intensity fluctuations mapped interferentially at 21 cm. Disturbance theory utilizes scalar and vector perturbations to derive intensity from fundamental long-wave density, velocity, and spin fields, revealing that the latter two contribute significantly to the intensity forecast. We illustrate this by presenting a simulation-based simulation demonstrating a visible correlation between spin orientation and observable intensity. We also present forward models that quantify foreground contamination as excess power at high angular scales (low $\ell$). Finally, we employ principal component analysis (PCA) to test various data cleaning strategies on the artificial dataset. The results show that while the interferometric signal is clearly visible in the output, foreground dominance at large scales necessitates rigorous data removal techniques.

A particle package is defined as a collection of multiple particles that interact via various forces, including self-interactions, while traveling together through space. Although numerous such packages exist in nature, they have not received sufficient attention regarding the various parameters influencing their emission processes. In this study, we investigate the microscopic mechanisms behind the emission of such packages at colliders, taking into account interactions governed by the strong, weak, and electromagnetic forces. It has been determined that, regardless of whether a package originates from a weak interaction vertex, the emission rate remains invariant under parity transformations, provided parity symmetry holds at its vertex of origin. Consequently, the parity-conservation rule dictates that any detector capable of distinguishing package emission directions relative to their mother particle's spin axis must observe an asymmetry in the number of emitted packages. Specifically, more packages should be detected preferentially in one spin-oriented hemisphere compared to the other.
